newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn unable to break budget jam, but progress made.
newsitem.headline: Bonn unable to break budget jam, but progress made.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government failed to break its deadlock on covering budget deficits at a meeting of coalition party leaders on Wednesday, but officials said there was some progress.

Coalition sources said that Kohl's Christian Democrats and the centrist Free Democrats were nearing an agreement to bring forward parts of a tax reform planned for 1999 to 1998 that would counter the effects of lower-than-expected tax revenues.

The plan, which also has support from the anti-tax FDP, would give the government nearly eight billion marks for 1998 and make it possible for the coalition to stick to a pledge to cut the so-called solidarity tax by two points to 5.5 percent.
Further savings would be realised by selling off about a dozen pieces of property currently owned by the government, the officials said.
They added that the two coalition partners were gradually making progress on their efforts to trim the budget deficits in 1997 and 1998, although a breakthrough agreement was still not in sight.
Bernd Protzner, general secretary of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), said that the sentiment in Germany that the government was in deep trouble would soon prove to be wrong.

Coalition officials said that the government was also considering eliminating tax breaks for corporate reserves already in 1998. The FDP would be willing to agree to that because it could not be considered a tax increase.
The plan would merely be closing existing loopholes while at the same time cutting manufacturing taxes. Ordinary taxpayers would not be affected, the officials said.
